explanations.explanation: The tombs it is. Jesus gets out of the boat and is met by a man who is coming from the tombs. Verse 3 adds that this man had been living there. I think this part of his story is a heavy one.
A city gate never shows up in this scene. Mark says the man was coming from the tombs when he met Jesus. The very next verse says he had been living there. So the gate stays out of the story.

A threshing floor is a place where farmers work their grain. Mark doesn't put the man anywhere near one. He says the man was coming from the tombs and had been living there. That's a fair guess for a farmer, though.
It's the other way around. The chains and shackles couldn't hold him. Mark says he "…had broken the chains and shattered the shackles." He was often bound, and it never lasted.

That's right. People bound him again and again, but Mark says he "…had broken the chains and shattered the shackles." Nothing they had could hold him. Keep that picture in your head, because it makes the next moment hit even harder.

Strength is the word. Mark says, "Now there was no one with the strength to subdue him." People had tried with chains and shackles, and none of it held. The chains were broken and the shackles shattered.

Patience is a good thing to have, but it isn't the word here. Mark says no one had the strength to subdue him. The chains had been broken and the shackles shattered. This was about what people could hold, not how long they could wait.
Permission isn't what's missing in this verse. Mark says, "Now there was no one with the strength to subdue him." The chains and shackles were broken and shattered. So the missing piece was strength.

Mark says it was more than nighttime. He says, "Night and day in the tombs and in the mountains he kept crying out and cutting himself with stones." I think this verse hurts. It was happening around the clock.

That's right. Mark says, "Night and day in the tombs and in the mountains he kept crying out and cutting himself with stones." It didn't stop when the sun came up. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story, and it's good to slow down for it.

explanations.answer: Runs and falls on his knees before Him
explanations.explanation: Exactly. When he saw Jesus from a distance, "…he ran and fell on his knees before Him." This is the man nobody could hold, and he ends up kneeling. Jesus had already told the spirit to come out of him.

explanations.answer: Runs at Him swinging his broken chains
explanations.explanation: Mark does say the chains were broken, back in verse 4. But when he sees Jesus, there is no swinging of chains. He runs and falls on his knees before Him. That's a very different picture.

explanations.answer: Picks up stones to throw at Him
explanations.explanation: Stones come up in this story, but not like that. Verse 5 says he cut himself with stones. When he sees Jesus from a distance, he ran and fell on his knees before Him. Nobody throws a single stone in this scene.

explanations.answer: Son of the Most High God
explanations.explanation: Yes. He shouts, "What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?" Out of everyone on that shore, he says it out loud. He knows exactly who just got out of that boat.

That's a real title for Jesus, and Bartimaeus uses it in Mark 10:47, but it isn't the one he shouts here. He says, "What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?" Same Jesus, different title. Mark's wording is the one that counts.
He doesn't say that. What comes out of him is, "What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?" That's a much bigger title than a prophet from a town. He is calling Jesus the Son of God.
True. He shouts, "I beg You before God not to torture me!" It's a strange thing to hear from a man who just ran up to Jesus. The next verse explains where it's coming from.
It's true, actually. Mark says he shouted, "I beg You before God not to torture me!" He begs, loudly. And verse 8 tells us what had already happened before he said it.
Yes. Mark says Jesus had already declared, "Come out of this man, you unclean spirit!" That's Jesus speaking, and He speaks to the spirit directly. Everything the man shouts comes after that.
Jesus doesn't tell the spirit to stay anywhere. He says, "Come out of this man, you unclean spirit!" It's a command to leave. Stay silent isn't in the verse.
The tombs are where the man had been living, but Jesus doesn't send the spirit there. He says, "Come out of this man, you unclean spirit!" The command is about the man, not the tombs.
Legion is the name. Jesus asks, and the answer is, "My name is Legion…" Short answer, but it says a lot. The rest of that verse tells us why that name fits.
That's a name from another place in the Gospels (Matthew 12:24), not this scene. Here the answer to Jesus is, "My name is Legion…" You'll find it right there in verse 9.
Abaddon doesn't show up in this story. When Jesus asks the name, the answer is, "My name is Legion…" That's the only name given. Good thing the text spells it out.
Many is right. He says, “for we are many.” That's the reason for the name Legion. The name is all about how many they are.
Mighty isn't the word here. The text says, “for we are many.” The name is about how many they are, not how strong.
Mark doesn't say anything about them being ancient. He says, “for we are many.” The reason for the name is their number. Nothing about age comes into it.
Region is the word. Mark says he begged Jesus repeatedly not to send them out of that region. They kept asking over and over.
That's close, but Mark says something different. He says they begged not to be sent out of that region. It's about the area, not the man. Good thing to catch on a second read.
The tombs are in this story, but that's not the word. Mark says he begged Jesus repeatedly not to send them out of that region. It's the whole area they're talking about, not one spot.
That's what they ask. The demons beg Jesus, "Send us to the pigs, so that we may enter them." They had begged not to be sent out of that region, and now they point to the herd on the hillside.

explanations.answer: Let us stay in the man
explanations.explanation: That's not their request. They beg, "Send us to the pigs, so that we may enter them." The herd on the hillside is the plan they bring to Jesus. The man isn't in that request.

explanations.answer: Send us back to the tombs
explanations.explanation: The tombs don't come up in this request. The demons beg, "Send us to the pigs, so that we may enter them." The pigs are on the nearby hillside. That's where they ask to go.
It's the other way around. Mark says, "He gave them permission, and the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs…" Jesus lets them go. Nobody had to guess.
That's right. Mark says, "He gave them permission, and the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs…" Jesus doesn't refuse. The unclean spirits come out of the man and go into the herd.

explanations.answer: Down the steep bank into the sea
explanations.explanation: Yes. The herd "…rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the water." That happened right after the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs. Jesus had given them permission.
The herd goes the opposite direction. Mark says they rushed down the steep bank into the sea. The mountains are mentioned earlier in the story, but the pigs don't go there.
The town hears about it later. The pigs rush down the steep bank into the sea. Those who were tending them ran off to the town afterward, not the pigs.
Thousand is right. Mark says the herd was "…about two thousand…" That's one very big herd. All of it rushed down the steep bank into the sea.
Two hundred is much smaller than what Mark says. He says the herd of about two thousand rushed down into the sea. That's a big herd on that hillside.
Two dozen is only twenty-four pigs, far fewer than Mark says. He says the herd was about two thousand. Big difference, baker.

explanations.answer: Sitting clothed and in his right mind
explanations.explanation: That's it. The people "…saw the man who had been possessed by the legion of demons sitting there, clothed and in his right mind…" Remember how he was described at the start? This is a very different picture, and Mark says it plainly.

explanations.answer: Lying on the ground unable to speak
explanations.explanation: That isn't how they find him. Mark says he was sitting there, clothed and in his right mind. He's not lying down, and nothing says he couldn't speak.
That's not the scene. The people find him sitting there, clothed and in his right mind. He had been crying out at the start of the story, but this is a very different moment.

True. Mark says they saw him "…sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid." It's a short line, and the text doesn't tell us anything more about why. I think that was a lot to take in.
They were afraid. Mark says they saw the man "…sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid." The text doesn't give a reason for their fear. So this one is True.

That's what they ask. Mark says, "…the people began to beg Jesus to leave their region." This comes after those who had seen it described what happened to the man and the pigs. The text doesn't say why they ask.
They ask for the opposite. Mark says the people began to beg Jesus to leave their region. Staying isn't part of it.
Healing isn't what they ask for here. Mark says the people began to beg Jesus to leave their region. That's the only request they make in this scene.
Yes. As Jesus is getting into the boat, the man "…begged to go with Him." He wants to be right there with Jesus. Mark doesn't give a reason, but I'd say that's easy to understand.
That isn't what he asks. Mark says he begged to go with Jesus. His own people come up later, when Jesus tells him to go home to them.
He asks for something different. The people were the ones asking Jesus to leave. The man begged to go with Him.
It goes the other way. Mark says, "But Jesus would not allow him." The man wanted to come along, and Jesus gives him a different job. That's coming up in the very next words.
That's right. Mark says, "But Jesus would not allow him." Instead Jesus says, “Go home to your own people…” The man doesn't get in the boat.
Lord is the first word. Jesus says, “…how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.” The man is told to share what the Lord has done.
Mercy is the second word. Jesus says, “…how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.” The man is sent to tell his own people about it.
Prophet isn't in this sentence. Jesus says the man should tell them how much the Lord has done for him. The word is Lord, not prophet.
Riches don't come up here. Jesus says to tell them what mercy He has shown him. Mercy is the word that fits the blank.
Judgment isn't what Jesus says. He tells the man to share what mercy He has shown him. Mercy is the word in verse 19.
That's right. Mark says the man "…began to proclaim throughout the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him." The Decapolis is the region he goes through. And everyone was amazed.
Galilee is a real place in the Gospels, but Mark doesn't send him there in this passage. The text says he proclaimed throughout the Decapolis. That's the region the man covers.
Judea is a real place too, but it's not where Mark puts him. The man proclaimed throughout the Decapolis. That's the name the text gives.
